Ravin
RAV-in
verb, noun
From the Old French ravine, violent seizure, and that from the Latin rapina, plunder — the root of rapine and rapacious. As a verb, to seize and devour with violence; as a noun, the prey so taken.

Biblical Definition

Ravin is violent seizure, and Scripture uses it of beasts, of men, and of shepherds who are secretly both. Jacob’s blessing on his youngest son is the first instance: “Benjamin shall ravin as a wolf: in the morning he shall devour the prey, and at night he shall divide the spoil” (Gen 49:27) — a prophecy fulfilled in the tribe’s fierce warlike history, and, some have thought, in Benjamin’s most famous son, who in the morning of his life made havock of the church and in the evening divided the spoil among the Gentiles. Nahum uses the noun of Nineveh, the lion’s den “filled with prey, and his dens with ravin” (Nah 2:12) — an empire described as a lair heaped with what it has torn. But the gravest use is our Lord’s: “Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves” (Mat 7:15). Two things are asserted at once — the outward appearance is genuinely sheeplike, and the inward nature is genuinely predatory. The warning would be pointless if the disguise were poor. Ezekiel says the same of Israel’s own rulers: “Her princes in the midst thereof are like wolves ravening the prey, to shed blood, and to destroy souls, to get dishonest gain” (Eze 22:27). The wolf inside the fold is not a stranger who broke in; he is in the midst thereof.

Webster 1828 Definition

To seize and devour with violence; also, the prey so seized. Used of beasts of prey and, in our Lord’s warning, of false teachers within the fold.

expand to see more

RAVIN, v.i. To prey with rapacity; to seize and devour violently.

RAVIN, n. Prey; plunder; food obtained by violence.

From the Old French ravine; Latin rapina, plunder, from rapere, to seize.

Of the same family as rapine, rapacious, and ravenous.

Ravening, ppr. Preying with rapacity, as a wolf (Mat 7:15).

Key Scripture

Gen 49:27 — "Benjamin shall ravin as a wolf: in the morning he shall devour the prey, and at night he shall divide the spoil."

Nah 2:12 — "The lion did tear in pieces enough for his whelps, and strangled for his lionesses, and filled his holes with prey, and his dens with ravin."

Mat 7:15 — "Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves."

Eze 22:27 — "Her princes in the midst thereof are like wolves ravening the prey, to shed blood, and to destroy souls, to get dishonest gain."

Modern Corruption

Mat 7:15 is commonly applied only to obvious heretics outside the church, when our Lord’s point is that the wolf is convincingly dressed as a sheep and is standing inside the fold.

expand to see more

The corruption is misdirected vigilance. Congregations are taught to watch for false teaching at a distance — the cult on the doorstep, the heresy in another denomination — and are given almost no help identifying a ravening wolf who is orthodox in statement, warm in manner, and already trusted. But our Lord’s warning presumes exactly that. Sheep’s clothing means the disguise works; and Ezekiel puts the wolves in the midst of the city, among her own princes. Paul told the Ephesian elders the same thing with tears: grievous wolves would enter in, not sparing the flock, and also of your own selves shall men arise. The danger is domestic.

Recover the plain sense: our Lord gives the test in the next breath — ye shall know them by their fruits. Not by their eloquence, their following, their results, or their doctrinal statement, but by their fruit, and Ezekiel names the fruit that betrays a wolf: shedding blood, destroying souls, and getting dishonest gain. Where a ministry consistently produces damaged people and enriched leaders, the sheep’s clothing is irrelevant. And note the mercy in the warning: the Shepherd tells the sheep about the wolves. He does not leave His flock to discover them by being eaten.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin rapina, plunder — violent seizure; the nature of the wolf beneath the sheep’s clothing.

expand to see more

Ravin — Old French ravine, Latin rapina, plunder, from rapere, to seize.

Kin to rapine, rapacious, and ravenous.

As a noun, the prey itself: his dens with ravin (Nah 2:12).

Gen 49:27: Benjamin ravening as a wolf, morning prey and evening spoil.

Mat 7:15: the clothing is convincing; the nature is predatory.

Usage

"Mat 7:15 assumes the disguise works — that is why a test is needed."

"Eze 22:27 places the ravening wolves among Israel’s own princes."

"The test is fruit, and dishonest gain is the fruit that betrays a wolf."
